# What is geospatial visualization?

Almost every dataset contains a location, and geospatial visualization turns that "where" into a map so that patterns become visible at a glance [@pebesma2023]. The classic example is John Snow's map of cholera deaths in London in 1854: the deaths clustered around one water pump, and the map made the pattern obvious [@snow1855]. Today the same idea supports store location choice, delivery planning, price maps, flood-risk zoning and disease tracking. Three ideas underlie every map. First, a place is described by *coordinates*, here longitude (east-west) and latitude (north-south) in the GPS system WGS 84. Second, spatial data are either *vector* data (points, lines and polygons) or *raster* data (a grid of cells with one value each) [@lovelace2025]. Third, the *colour scale* decides what the reader sees.

# Case study: Zealandia

Zealandia is a good teaching case because the pattern is dramatic. It is a *proposed* continent of about 4.9 million km², of which roughly 94% lies under water; only New Zealand and New Caledonia rise above the sea [@mortimer2017]. It is not formally recognised by an official body. Mortimer et al. [-@mortimer2017] argue that it meets the geological tests for a continent: it is elevated above the surrounding ocean floor, has distinct geology, forms a well-defined area and has thicker crust than the ocean floor.

# Data and tools

The General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO) provides one global elevation grid for land and sea floor [@gebco]. It is a raster: each cell stores a longitude, a latitude and one value, the *elevation in metres relative to sea level* (positive = land, negative = sea floor). The resolution is 15 arc-seconds, so the South Pacific alone contains tens of millions of cells. Two tiles (155°E to 180° and 180° to 165°W, 10°S to 60°S) were downloaded so that Zealandia is complete on both sides of the date line. The analysis uses R [@rcore], the package `terra` for rasters [@terra] and `ggplot2` for drawing [@ggplot2].

# Method: from raster to map

Three steps matter. First, tiles east of the date line use negative longitudes, so they are shifted by 360° to make the Pacific one continuous map. Second, averaging blocks of 10 × 10 cells (about 2.5 arc-minutes) keeps the map sharp but fast to draw. Third, the colour scale is the main design decision: sea and land get different hues, and the break at 0 m is a clear shoreline.

```{r}
#| label: load
#| echo: true
#| eval: !expr has_data
files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.(tif|tiff|nc)$",
                    ignore.case = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
tiles <- lapply(files, function(f) {
  r <- rast(f)
  if (xmin(r) < 0) r <- shift(r, dx = 360)
  r
})
elev <- if (length(tiles) == 1) tiles[[1]] else do.call(merge, tiles)
names(elev) <- "elev"
elev_s <- aggregate(elev, fact = 10, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
df <- as.data.frame(elev_s, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
names(df) <- c("lon", "lat", "elev")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| echo: true
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| fig-cap: "Elevation of the South Pacific around Zealandia (GEBCO). The white line marks 2,500 m depth; the dashed line is a simplified outline."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
br   <- c(-10500, -6000, -4000, -2000, -1000, -200, 0, 500, 1500, 3800)
cols <- c("#030b2e", "#0a2463", "#1b4f9c", "#2f80c9", "#5db0e6",
          "#b5e3f5", "#efe6b8", "#7fb069", "#a67c52", "#ffffff")
zx <- c(160, 164, 169, 172, 175, 179, 183, 185, 184,
        178, 167, 165, 167, 166, 162, 159, 160)
zy <- c(-22, -19, -20, -25, -31, -36, -41, -46, -50,
        -54, -55, -50, -45, -40, -35, -29, -22)
outline <- data.frame(lon = zx, lat = zy)
lon_lab <- function(x) {
  ifelse(x > 180, paste0(360 - x, "W"), paste0(x, "E"))
}
lat_lab <- function(y) paste0(abs(y), "S")

ggplot(df, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = elev)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = cols, values = rescale(br),
                       limits = range(br), oob = squish,
                       name = "Elevation (m)") +
  geom_contour(aes(z = elev), breaks = -2500,
               colour = "white", linewidth = .25) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = elev), breaks = 0,
               colour = "black", linewidth = .25) +
  geom_path(data = outline, aes(lon, lat), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            colour = "#0fffd0", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = lon_lab, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = lat_lab, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_quickmap() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

# Reading the map

@fig-map shows three patterns. First, *shallow continental regions*: pale blue plateaus (Lord Howe Rise in the west, Campbell Plateau in the south, Chatham Rise in the east) stand far above the dark ocean floor around them. Second, *deep basins and trenches*: the Tasman Basin, the South Fiji Basin and the Kermadec Trench are the darkest blues. Third, *visible islands*: only the beige-to-brown cells, New Zealand and New Caledonia, are above 0 m.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-classes
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| tbl-cap: "Share of the simplified Zealandia outline by depth class"
zpoly <- vect(cbind(id = 1, part = 1, x = zx, y = zy), type = "polygons", crs = "EPSG:4326")
roi <- as.data.frame(c(mask(elev_s, zpoly), cellSize(elev_s, unit = "km")), na.rm = TRUE)
names(roi) <- c("elev", "area_km2")
roi$Class <- cut(roi$elev, c(-Inf, -5000, -2500, -200, 0, Inf),
  labels = c("Deep basin (< -5,000 m)", "Slope (-5,000 to -2,500 m)",
             "Platform (-2,500 to -200 m)", "Shelf (-200 to 0 m)", "Land (> 0 m)"))
tab <- roi |> group_by(Class) |>
  summarise(`Area (million km²)` = round(sum(area_km2) / 1e6, 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(`Share (%)` = round(100 * `Area (million km²)` / sum(`Area (million km²)`), 1))
knitr::kable(tab)
```

@tbl-classes turns the colours into numbers: the share of land should be small (the published figure is about 6%), while the platform class dominates. The elevation distribution in @fig-hist explains why.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of elevation. The two humps are the shallow platform and the deep ocean floor."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
set.seed(1)
ggplot(df[sample(nrow(df), min(nrow(df), 2e5)), ], aes(elev)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100, fill = "#2f80c9") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-2500, 0), linetype = c("dashed", "solid")) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Cells") + theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

The histogram is *bimodal*: one hump of cells at moderate depth (the continental platform) and another much deeper (the oceanic basins), with very few cells near 0 m. A continent that is submerged in this way shows up as a plateau, not as land.

# Limitations and further resources

The outline used here is a simplified polygon, not an official boundary, and the 2,500 m contour is only a teaching proxy: the true boundary is defined by geology, not by one depth [@mortimer2017]. Averaging cells reduces detail, and cells shrink toward the poles, which is why the table uses `cellSize()` for areas. For further reading, *Geocomputation with R* [@lovelace2025] and *Spatial Data Science* [@pebesma2023] cover vector and raster data in depth, and *R for Data Science* [@r4ds] covers the `ggplot2` basics.

# Exercise for beginners: put yourself on the map

No R experience is needed, and nothing has to be installed: the exercise runs in the browser (QR code in @fig-qr). The starter code (on the exercise page) draws the world, Zealandia in turquoise and three places. Participants (1) press *Run Code*, (2) replace "Chennai" and its numbers by their hometown, (3) change the colour `"red"`, and (4) add a fourth place. Longitude is counted from 0° to 360° so that Zealandia stays in one piece.

```{r}
#| label: fig-exercise
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Output of the starter code: the world, Zealandia (turquoise) and three places."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 2.9
library(maps)
cities <- data.frame(name = c("Cologne", "Wellington", "Chennai"),
                     lon = c(6.96, 174.78, 80.27), lat = c(50.94, -41.29, 13.08))
zx <- c(160,164,169,172,175,179,183,185,184,178,167,165,167,166,162,159,160)
zy <- c(-22,-19,-20,-25,-31,-36,-41,-46,-50,-54,-55,-50,-45,-40,-35,-29,-22)
map("world2", xlim = c(0, 360), ylim = c(-65, 80), fill = TRUE, col = "#9bd17a", bg = "#0f4c81",
    border = "#3f7d3f", lwd = .3, mar = c(.5, .5, .5, .5))
polygon(zx, zy, col = rgb(.05, .95, .8, .55), border = "#0fffd0", lwd = 2)
points(cities$lon, cities$lat, pch = 21, bg = "red", col = "white", cex = 1.6)
text(cities$lon, cities$lat + 7, cities$name, font = 2, cex = .8)
```
